summary: Describes methods for carrying Chinese characters in Internet text services such as email, network news, Telnet and the web. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Computers needed a way to write Chinese letters in messages that only knew simple characters. This explains how to wrap them so they arrive safely.

questions: how to encode chinese characters in email
chinese character encoding for internet messages
why is iso-2022-cn better for email than 8-bit encodings
subtitle: Methods for encoding Chinese characters in Internet text services.

tldr.problem: Internet text services (email, news, Telnet, web) were designed for ASCII characters and could not safely transmit Chinese characters, which require multi-byte representations.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1922 defines several encoding schemes: ISO-2022-CN and ISO-2022-CN-EXT (7-bit, using escape sequences to switch between ASCII and Chinese character sets), and CN-GB and CN-Big5 (8-bit encodings using the high bit to distinguish Chinese from ASCII).
tldr.outcome: These encodings enabled interchange of Chinese text across the Internet, with ISO-2022-CN becoming the standard for interoperability due to its 7-bit nature that works with all mail systems.

today: RFC 1922 is an Informational document that remains historically important for understanding how Chinese text was transported in early Internet services. It has not been obsoleted, though modern systems now typically use UTF-8 Unicode encoding for Chinese characters rather than the ISO-2022 or 8-bit encodings described here.

sections.title: The Need for Chinese Character Encoding
sections.content:
The Internet was initially designed for English text, using ASCII which represents 128 characters. Chinese uses tens of thousands of characters, making it impossible to map them to ASCII. When the Internet expanded to China, Taiwan, and other Chinese-speaking regions, a way was needed to transport Chinese text through email, network news, Telnet, and the World Wide Web.

The challenge is that many Internet services handle only 7-bit ASCII text safely. Any encoding must either work within the 7-bit constraint or require 8-bit transport infrastructure (which may not be available on all networks). Additionally, there are multiple Chinese character standards: simplified characters (used in mainland China) and traditional characters (used in Taiwan and Hong Kong), along with different internal computer codes like GB, Big5, and CNS 11643.
sections.eli5: When computers started spreading to China, they had a big problem: Chinese has thousands of characters, but the Internet only knew 26 letters and some numbers. They had to figure out how to fit Chinese into a system designed for English.

sections.title: ISO-2022-CN: The 7-bit Solution
sections.content:
ISO-2022-CN is based on the ISO 2022 standard and works like earlier standards for Japanese (ISO-2022-JP) and Korean (ISO-2022-KR). It is a 7-bit encoding, meaning it uses only standard ASCII bytes (0-127) and works with any mail system, even those that strip the 8th bit from bytes.

ISO-2022-CN uses designations (special escape sequences) to declare which character set is active, and shifts to switch between ASCII and Chinese characters. For example, the escape sequence ESC $ ) A designates GB 2312-80 (simplified Chinese), and the shift SO (shift out, byte 0x0E) switches to that character set. SI (shift in, byte 0x0F) switches back to ASCII. Each line starts in ASCII and must end in ASCII before the newline.

ISO-2022-CN supports both GB 2312-80 (simplified) and CNS 11643 plane 1 and 2 (traditional), so it can represent both forms of Chinese within a single message. The extended version, ISO-2022-CN-EXT, adds support for additional GB and CNS character planes.
sections.eli5: This clever trick uses special invisible codes to tell the computer 'now I'm typing Chinese characters' and 'now I'm back to English.' Every line starts and ends in English, and uses escape codes to switch in the middle. It works on any email system because it only uses the basic ASCII bytes.

sections.title: 8-bit Encodings: CN-GB and CN-Big5
sections.content:
CN-GB and CN-Big5 are 8-bit internal code encodings for Chinese. They are simpler than ISO-2022-CN but require 8-bit transport and stronger support for encoding in MIME headers.

CN-GB uses GB 2312-80 character set with a simple scheme: if the high bit (MSB) of a byte is 0, it is ASCII; if the MSB is 1, it is a Chinese character (two such bytes represent one character). CN-Big5, widely used in Taiwan, follows a similar pattern: ASCII characters have MSB 0, and Big5 characters (two bytes each) have MSB 1 in the first byte. Both require declaring the encoding in the MIME charset parameter (e.g., charset=cn-gb or charset=cn-big5).

When sent over the Internet, these 8-bit encodings require either the 8-bit SMTP extension or a Content-Transfer-Encoding like BASE64 or QUOTED-PRINTABLE on networks that do not handle 8-bit data cleanly. ISO-2022-CN is preferred for maximum interoperability because it requires no such extension.
sections.eli5: These simpler encodings just say 'if a byte has its high bit turned on, it's Chinese, otherwise it's English.' It's easy to decode but only works on systems that handle 8-bit bytes safely, so emails have to wrap the Chinese in an extra layer sometimes.

sections.title: Supporting Multiple Chinese Encoding Standards
sections.content:
Chinese computing uses several different character standards that were developed independently: GB (mainland China's standard), Big5 (traditional characters, mostly Taiwan), and CNS 11643 (Taiwan's formal standard). Additionally, variants like GB 12345-90 (traditional form of GB) and extensions like ISO-IR-165 (GB 2312 plus GB 8565) exist.

RFC 1922 notes that ISO-2022-CN and ISO-2022-CN-EXT can facilitate interchange between these systems. For example, Big5 can be supported using ISO-2022-CN because the first two planes of CNS 11643 contain the same characters as Big5's most common part (with only two duplicate character differences). The RFC includes a conversion table for mapping Big5 to CNS-11643, allowing Big5 text to be represented in ISO-2022-CN format for network interchange.

The document also introduces new MIME parameters: charset-edition (e.g., 1980) to distinguish different editions of the same character standard, and charset-extension for vendor-specific extensions of standards.
sections.eli5: Different countries and companies developed their own ways of writing Chinese on computers. This RFC explains how to convert between them and add notes in email headers about which version you're using, so the person receiving your email knows how to read it.

sections.title: Status and Recommendations
sections.content:
For maximum interoperability, implementations are recommended to support sending and receiving ISO-2022-CN at minimum. Supporting all character sets in ISO-2022-CN-EXT is encouraged for broader compatibility. While CN-GB and CN-Big5 are used internally on many systems, sending messages in ISO-2022-CN format is preferred for network interchange to ensure safe delivery across all mail systems.

The RFC also mentions Unicode (ISO/IEC 10646), which includes all the characters from GB, CNS, and other Chinese standards in a single universal space. However, at the time of publication (March 1996), Unicode support in email systems was not yet widespread, so the ISO-2022 and 8-bit encodings described here were essential for practical Chinese Internet communication.
sections.eli5: For the best chance that everyone can read your Chinese email, use ISO-2022-CN because it works everywhere. The other methods are faster if your email system is set up for 8-bit, but they might not work if your email goes through old computers that only understand 7-bit text.

items.label: SO designation for GB 2312-80
items.desc: Designates GB 2312-80 (simplified Chinese) for use with SO shift.

items.label: SO designation for CNS 11643-1
items.desc: Designates CNS 11643 plane 1 (traditional Chinese) for use with SO shift.

items.label: SS2 designation for CNS 11643-2
items.desc: Designates CNS 11643 plane 2 for use with SS2 shift (two bytes at a time).

items.label: Shift Out
items.desc: Switches subsequent bytes to the SO-designated character set.
